cities.name: Sydney
cities.transportNote: In Sydney you can also pay by tapping your contactless bank card or your phone, not just with an Opal card.

cities.transportNote: Adelaide Metro offers contactless tap-and-pay: you may not need to buy a card when you arrive. Check on their site which services accept it.
cities.rsaNote: In Adelaide the RSA course is delivered by registered providers: look for one that offers the responsible service of alcohol unit of competency and confirm it's registered before you pay.

urgent.label: Urgent
urgent.msg: Your priority is a cheap place to live that you can verify, and your first income. Justo has reordered your list for that.
urgent.title: If your money lasts less than 4 weeks
tips: **Housing:** choose the cheapest option you can verify. A shared dorm or a room in a shared house usually costs less than a studio. Don't transfer money without seeing the place or having a contract.
**Food:** cook for yourself. Compare the price per kilo or per litre on the label and buy the basics: rice, pasta, eggs, legumes, and seasonal fruit and vegetables.
**Transport:** walk or cycle when you can. Many systems have a daily or weekly fare cap: check the one in your city.
**Work:** your first job doesn't have to be the ideal one, it has to pay the rent. Apply for entry-level jobs (kitchen, cleaning, warehouse, delivery, shops) while you look for something better.
**Check your numbers every week.** If your cushion is getting shorter, look for local help before you run out completely.

tight.label: Tight
tight.msg: You have enough for a few weeks, but not for mistakes. Compare options before you pay and start looking for work from day one.
tight.title: If your money lasts between 4 and 8 weeks
tips: **Compare at least three housing options** before you pay the deposit (bond).
**Set aside the money for the bond and rent in advance first.** Spend on extras only after that.
**Set a weekly limit for food and transport** and check how much you spent every Sunday.
**Look for work from day one:** every week sooner you manage to start, your cushion goes back up.

comfortable.label: Comfortable
comfortable.msg: You have room to choose calmly. Use it to avoid rushed decisions, not to put off the job search.
comfortable.title: If your money lasts more than 8 weeks
tips: **Choose calmly, but don't delay your job search:** the best offers take time.
**Set aside an emergency fund** (for example, 4 weeks of expenses) and don't touch it.
**Avoid overpaying for convenience** in the first days (transport, eating out): the cost of living is high.

short.label: Urgent
short.msg: Your one-off payments are higher than your money. Lower the deposit (a different room or type of housing) or arrive with more funds before you commit.

phases.title: Before you travel
phases.sub: What's worth sorting out before you board the plane: where you'll sleep, how you'll get around, how much money you have and what you can bring.

tasks.text: Book your accommodation for the first week and keep the address and the confirmation.
tasks.why: Without an address you can't receive your TFN letter, open an account or send applications. Book something with flexible cancellation (a hostel or a room) and look for something better once you're in the city.
tasks.warn: Don't pay for a place you can't verify: ask for real photos, a video call and the booking or contract in writing.
tasks.urgent: Choose the cheapest option you can verify: a shared dorm in a hostel or a room in a shared house.

tasks.text: Plan how you'll get from the airport to your accommodation and how you'll pay for transport.
tasks.why: Look at the route, the cost and the timetable before you land. Save screenshots of the map, the address and the place's phone number in case you have no data when you arrive. Arriving tired and without a plan is when people overpay the most.

tasks.text: Contact someone who's already in {city}: family, friends or a Facebook group from your country.
tasks.why: A local saves you weeks of trial and error: they can tell you which suburbs and transport to use, where people look for work and what to avoid. Write to them before you travel and ask one specific question. If you don't know anyone, look for groups of migrants from your country in your city and ask for advice by message.
tasks.warn: Verify anyone you meet online (video call, references) before sending them money or documents.

tasks.text: Work out your cushion: how many weeks you can live on the money you're bringing.
tasks.why: Every week in Australia costs rent, food and transport. Knowing your number before you travel decides what to prioritise: with little money, Justo puts a cheap place to live and your first income first.

tasks.text: Check what you can bring and what you must declare: alcohol, tobacco, food, medicines and cash.
tasks.why: Alcohol and tobacco have limits for bringing them in duty-free. As a reference, for adults (18 or over) it's 2.25 litres of alcohol and 25 cigarettes or 25 g of tobacco; confirm the current limits on the official website. Food, plants and animal products are tightly controlled (biosecurity). If you carry AUD 10,000 or more in cash, you must declare it. Nicotine vapes and many medicines have their own rules.
tasks.warn: When in doubt, declare it on the arrival card (Incoming Passenger Card). Not declaring something you should have declared can be expensive: fines and delays.

links.label: ABF: can I bring it in?

tasks.text: Bring an international card and some cash in AUD for your first days.
tasks.why: You need to pay for transport, a SIM and food before you have an Australian account. Some banks let you start opening an account before you arrive: check their guides for newcomers. To send money from your home country, compare fees and exchange rates.
tasks.warn: Don't carry large amounts of cash: from AUD 10,000 (or the equivalent) you must declare it.

tasks.text: Prepare your CV in the Australian style, in English (1 or 2 pages).
tasks.why: It's the fastest way to get closer to an income: if you arrive with your CV ready, you can apply from day 1. In Australia a CV normally doesn't include a photo, age or marital status; it does include experience, skills, availability and references.

links.label: Workforce Australia: how to write your CV

tasks.text: Check the conditions of your student visa: work, attendance and changing course.
tasks.why: Work and study conditions can change. Confirm the current ones in your account (VEVO) and with Home Affairs; don't rely on what you're told on WhatsApp.

links.label: Study Australia: guide to the 500 visa

tasks.text: Understand your Working Holiday conditions: 6 months with the same employer and which work counts towards extending the visa.
tasks.why: The usual limit is 6 months with the same employer. Some jobs (for example, certain farm work in regional areas) may count towards applying for a second visa. Confirm the exceptions and what qualifies with Home Affairs before you accept a job.

tasks.text: Confirm the conditions of your visa and of your sponsoring employer.
tasks.why: Your visa usually ties you to an employer and an occupation: confirm what you can and can't do. No legitimate person can charge you for sponsoring you or ask you to pay back part of your salary.

tasks.text: Arrange your health cover for students (OSHC).
tasks.why: Your visa requires it for the whole time you study. It covers general doctor visits, part of hospital costs, ambulance and some medicines; it normally doesn't cover dental or optical. Keep your proof of cover.

tasks.text: Check your health cover: Medicare only applies to some countries and visas.
tasks.why: Medicare is for certain residents and for visitors from countries with health agreements with Australia. If you don't qualify, you need private insurance: without cover, a hospital visit can cost a lot.

links.label: Medicare for temporary residents covered by a Ministerial Order

tasks.text: Put your documents together in a digital folder and a printed one.
tasks.why: You'll be asked for them when you open an account, rent and apply for jobs: passport and visa grant letter, proof of accommodation and insurance, degrees and certificates (translated if needed), work references, driver's licence and medical prescriptions. If you're a student, also your confirmation of enrolment (CoE).
tasks.warn: Keep digital copies somewhere private, with a password. Don't send photos of your passport to anyone who isn't an official body or a provider you've already verified.

tasks.text: Unlock your phone and decide how you'll get mobile data when you land.
tasks.why: With mobile data you have maps, transport, banking and messages from day one. If your phone is still locked to a carrier from your country, it won't work with an Australian SIM. You can buy a prepaid SIM when you arrive or install an eSIM before you travel, if your phone supports it.

phases.title: Days 1–3
phases.sub: What can't wait: sleeping safely, having a phone, getting around and starting to look for work.

tasks.text: Settle in and confirm in writing the rules, the payment and what your accommodation includes.
tasks.why: Ask how much the deposit (bond) is and how it's returned, which bills are included (power, internet), how long you can stay and whether there's a contract or receipt. Take photos of the condition of the room when you move in.

tasks.text: Activate a prepaid SIM (or eSIM) to have data and an Australian number.
tasks.why: Employers will call or text that number: put it on your CV. Compare the price per month, not just the gigabytes.

tasks.text: Get your way to pay for transport and learn your main route.
tasks.urgent: Walk or cycle when you can. Many systems have a daily or weekly fare cap: check the one for your city on the official site.

tasks.text: Open an Australian bank account.
tasks.why: You need it to get paid, pay the rental deposit and use your card without fees. They normally ask for a passport, visa and an address in Australia; the requirements vary by bank. Compare monthly fees before you choose.

tasks.text: Apply for your TFN (tax file number) on the official ATO website.
tasks.why: Without a TFN, more tax can be withheld from your pay. It's free and you apply online in about 20 minutes, once you're in Australia. The letter with your number arrives by post at your mailing address and can take up to 28 days.
tasks.warn: No legitimate person charges you for it. Use only the official ATO site.
tasks.urgent: Don't wait for the letter before looking for work. Apply on day 1 or 2 so the letter arrives as soon as possible.

tasks.text: Make your job plan and turn on alerts on Seek, Indeed and Jora.
tasks.why: Every week without income eats into your cushion. Start today, even if you haven't settled in yet: the questionnaire gives you keywords, search links and the certificates your sector asks for.

tasks.text: Do your first basic shop and find the nearest supermarket.
tasks.why: Compare the price per kilo or per litre shown on the label, not just the price of the product.
tasks.urgent: Cook at home: rice, pasta, eggs, legumes and seasonal vegetables go further than ready-made food. Charity thrift shops (op shops) are good for pots, clothes and warm layers.

tasks.text: Save 000 for emergencies and share your address with someone you trust.
tasks.why: In an emergency (police, ambulance or fire) call 000. Let your family know where you are and how to reach you.

phases.title: Week 1
phases.sub: Secure a stable place and start applying seriously. Every week without income eats into your cushion.

tasks.text: Look for a stable rental in {city} before your temporary accommodation ends.
tasks.why: Learn your state's renting rules first: a written contract, the bond lodged with the official body (ask for the receipt) and how much they can ask for in advance. Search on Flatmates, Domain or realestate.com.au and in local groups, and see the place before you pay. Comparing three options avoids rushed decisions.
tasks.urgent: With little money, a room in a shared house is usually the cheapest. Ask how much the bond and the rent in advance are before going to see it: if you can't afford it, don't waste your time.

tasks.text: Apply every day and hand in your CV in person at businesses near you.
tasks.why: In hospitality, retail and cleaning many employers hire whoever turns up with a CV and a good attitude. Use your job plan to know where to look and what to say.

tasks.text: Write down what you spent this week and update your cushion.
tasks.why: Real numbers almost always differ from estimates. Adjust rent, food and transport to know how much time you have left.

tasks.text: Note where to ask for emergency help (food, housing and money) before you need it.
tasks.why: There are free emergency food and housing services. If you're a student, your institution usually has support for students in difficulty. Asking for help early costs less than waiting until you have nothing left.

links.label: Ask Izzy: free services near you

tasks.text: Get only the certificates the job you want asks for (RSA, White Card or others).
tasks.why: The RSA is for serving alcohol and the White Card for construction sites. They're short courses that cost money: do them when an employer asks or when you know they open up work in your area, and check the provider is registered.
tasks.urgent: If money is short, don't pay for certificates just in case: first get the job offer or confirmation that you need it.

tasks.text: Know your basic workplace rights and who to call if something isn't right.
tasks.why: All workers in Australia, whatever their visa, have the right to the minimum wage, a payslip and a safe workplace. Fair Work Ombudsman: 13 13 94, and you can call 13 14 50 first to ask for a free interpreter.
tasks.warn: Fair Work says your visa isn't cancelled for contacting them or asking for help. Even so, working outside your visa conditions can have immigration consequences: if in doubt, talk to a registered migration agent.

links.label: Fair Work: pay and conditions calculator

tasks.text: Learn the most common warning signs of scams in renting, work and money.
tasks.why: Be wary if they ask you to pay before you see the place, offer you a very well paid job without an interview, ask you to transfer money or pressure you to decide now. Check the offer through another channel. If in doubt: stop, check and protect yourself.

tasks.text: Join a group from your community and go to an event this week.
tasks.why: Meeting people gives you first-hand information, job offers that aren't advertised and support when you miss home. Look for groups from your country in your city, events at your institution or activities on Meetup.

phases.title: Weeks 2–4
phases.sub: Consolidate your income and avoid overpaying.

tasks.text: Keep the pace: apply daily and follow up on what you've sent.
tasks.why: Most entry-level jobs are won through volume and persistence. Once a week, review what worked and adjust your CV and keywords.

tasks.text: In your first job: give your TFN, choose your super fund and ask for your contract.
tasks.why: Your employer will ask for your TFN and your bank account details: hand them over as soon as you have them so they don't withhold more tax. Ask which super fund they'll use or choose one yourself. Ask in writing for your hours and your hourly rate.

tasks.text: Keep your payslips, your contract and a record of your hours.
tasks.why: They help with your tax return and to claim if something doesn't add up. Note your hours each week, even if your employer also keeps track.

tasks.text: Keep track of your work hours against the current conditions of your visa.
tasks.why: Going over the hours limit on your student visa can put your visa at risk. Justo doesn't quote figures because they change: check your current limit in VEVO and with Home Affairs, and keep a weekly count.

links.label: Study Australia: working while you study
Fair Work: guide for international students

tasks.text: Keep count of your months with each employer.
tasks.why: On a Working Holiday you can normally work up to 6 months with the same employer. Check the exceptions and which work counts towards a second visa before you accept.

tasks.text: Keep your rental agreement, the bond receipt and your payment receipts.
tasks.why: You'll need them to get your bond back when you move out and to prove your address to the bank and for other paperwork.

tasks.text: Compare your real spending with your budget and cut what isn't essential.
tasks.why: Review rent, food, transport and subscriptions. A small, steady cut stretches your cushion further than it seems.

tasks.text: Find a general practitioner (GP) and keep your OSHC insurance details.
tasks.why: With OSHC you can see a GP who accepts your insurer. Ask whether they bill your insurer directly or whether you pay and claim a refund. Keep your card number and your insurer's phone number.

tasks.text: Find a clinic and a general practitioner (GP), and understand what it costs to go without cover.
tasks.why: Without Medicare, a visit can cost quite a bit more and a hospital much more. Keep your insurance number and Healthdirect's (1800 022 222) handy for health advice.

tasks.text: If you need to improve your English, look for free or low-cost classes.
tasks.why: Libraries, community centres and many councils offer free or cheap conversation and English classes. Practising the phrases in the Resources tab before an interview also helps.

tasks.text: Check whether you're eligible for free English classes through the AMEP program.
tasks.why: The Adult Migrant English Program offers free classes to eligible migrants. Confirm your eligibility based on your visa.

phases.title: Month 2 onwards
phases.sub: Sort out tax, visa and savings, and think about your next step.

tasks.text: Understand your tax and create your myGov account.
tasks.why: The Australian tax year runs from 1 July to 30 June. If you worked, you normally lodge a tax return at the end of the tax year. Your rules depend on your visa and whether you're a tax resident: check the ATO guide for your case.

tasks.text: Check your visa in VEVO and, if you need immigration help, use only a registered agent.
tasks.why: Only registered migration agents (MARA) can give immigration advice. Be wary of anyone who guarantees results or asks for cash payments without a receipt.

links.label: MARA: how to choose an agent

tasks.text: Learn how your super works and what happens to it if you leave Australia.
tasks.why: Your employer pays super on top of your wages. If you leave Australia, you may be able to claim it as a DASP (Departing Australia Superannuation Payment), depending on your visa. Keep your fund's details.

tasks.text: Look after your mental health: adjusting to a new country is tiring, and there is free help.
tasks.why: Missing home, money pressure and the language are normal. If you feel overwhelmed, talking to someone helps. Lifeline (13 11 14) and Beyond Blue (1300 22 4636) take calls from anyone.

tasks.text: Start an emergency fund: aim to cover at least 4 weeks of expenses.
tasks.why: It's a Justo rule of thumb, not an official rule. With that margin you can lose a shift, change jobs or pay for an emergency without panicking.

tasks.text: Define your next step: a better job, study or local experience.
tasks.why: With local experience and Australian references your CV carries more weight. Ask your supervisors for references, update your CV with concrete achievements and explore openings in your field.

tasks.text: Tell us what helped and what was missing.
tasks.why: Justo gets better with your experience. What you send is private: it isn't published.
tasks.warn: Don't include your passport, TFN, account numbers or anything you don't want to share.

work.intro: Answer five questions and Justo builds a plan to land your first job as soon as possible. Your answers stay on this device.

sectors.label: Cafés, restaurants and bars
certs: RSA (Responsible Service of Alcohol): required to serve alcohol. You get it with a course in your state.
Basic food hygiene: some venues ask for it for kitchen work; many teach it when you start.
tips: Take your CV printed and hand it in person, preferably outside peak hours (mid-afternoon usually works well).
Kitchen hand is an entry point that needs little English.
Say from the start which days and times you can work: in hospitality, availability counts for a lot.
A trial should be short and used to assess your skills. If they put you to work as an employee, they must pay you.

sectors.label: Shops and supermarkets
tips: Customer service counts for more than experience: practise a short introduction in English.
Big chains usually take applications in the careers section of their website; small shops, in person.
Ask about weekend and evening shifts: they're usually the easiest to get.

sectors.label: Cleaning
tips: A good entry point if your English is still basic. Many shifts are early in the morning or at night.
Ask for a contract (or offer letter) and a payslip, even if you're paid in cash.
Cleaning companies hire by area: look for the ones in your neighbourhood and ask how to get to the workplace.

sectors.label: Warehouse and logistics
certs: Forklift licence (High Risk Work licence): only if you want to operate a forklift. For picking and packing it's normally not required.
tips: Temp agencies cover many warehouse shifts. Registering is free: never pay for a job offer.
Ask how to get there without a car; many warehouses are far from public transport.
Bring safety footwear if they ask for it: ask who pays for it before you buy it.

sectors.label: Delivery and driving
certs: A driver's licence valid in your state. Check how you can use a foreign licence and whether you need an international permit.
tips: Many delivery apps hire you as a contractor, not an employee. Before you start, confirm with Home Affairs whether that work is compatible with your visa and whether it counts towards your hours limit.
Work out the real cost (fuel, insurance, wear on the vehicle) before deciding whether it's worth it.

sectors.label: Construction and maintenance
certs: White Card (construction safety induction): required to enter a building site. The course is short.
tips: Without a White Card you can't enter a site. Get it once you have an offer or know for certain you need it.
If they ask for an ABN (business number) instead of hiring you, get advice before accepting: it could be a sham contracting arrangement.
Physical work is appreciated: say so and show a good attitude.

sectors.label: Care work
certs: They usually ask for a police check and, depending on the role, care training, first aid and other credentials.
tips: It needs more fluent English and patience. There is a lot of demand, but also more requirements.
Ask which courses or checks you need before starting and who pays for them.

sectors.label: Farm and rural work
tips: On a Working Holiday, some farm work in regional areas can count towards a second visa. Check with Home Affairs which work and which areas qualify before accepting.
Get in writing how you'll be paid (hourly or per piece), where you'll sleep and what they deduct. Be wary if they ask for money to get the job.
Conditions can be tough and the place can be remote: ask about transport and accommodation.

sectors.label: Office and professional work
tips: They expect solid English. LinkedIn and Seek are the main channels: tailor your CV to each listing.
If your profession is regulated (engineering, health, education, etc.), ask what recognition of your qualification you need.
While the ideal offer arrives, keep applying for quick-entry jobs too.

english.label: Basic: I understand little and find it hard to speak
english.advice: Start with jobs where little talking is needed: kitchen, cleaning, warehouse or farm work. Take your CV, practise the phrases in Resources and don't wait until you "speak well" to start: your English improves faster by working. Look for free or cheap classes too.

english.label: Intermediate: I get by with simple sentences
english.advice: You can aim for cafés, shops and delivery. Prepare a two-minute introduction in English: who you are, what you can do and when you can start.

english.label: Advanced: I can hold a conversation and do an interview
english.advice: Aim higher: customer service, office and professional roles. Use LinkedIn and tailor your CV to each listing. Keep applying for quick-entry jobs too in case you need income while the ideal offer arrives.

availability.label: Flexible: nights, weekends and split shifts
availability.advice: Put it in the first line of your message or your CV: in hospitality, shops and warehouses, availability makes you more attractive.

availability.label: Limited: I have classes or other commitments
availability.advice: Look for casual or few-hours jobs and give your availability from the start. Check that the hours fit your visa conditions.

availability.label: Full: I can work full time
availability.advice: Aim for permanent roles or ones with regular shifts. If your visa limits your hours, confirm it before accepting.

licence.label: Yes, I have a driver's licence
licence.advice: Delivery and driving jobs open up. Check how you can use your foreign licence in your state.

licence.label: I don't have a licence
licence.advice: Prioritise jobs that are reachable by public transport and close to where you live: transport is a cost and a schedule.

before: An Australian-style CV in English (1 or 2 pages, no photo or age).
An Australian phone number and an email address with your real name.
Your visa at hand, and clarity on which jobs and how many hours it allows.
TFN applied for (you can start without it, but hand it over as soon as you have it).
A bank account so you can get paid.
A stable address where you can receive mail.
The certificates your sector asks for (see below).

plan.text: Get your CV, your email and your Australian phone ready.
Turn on job alerts with your keywords on Seek, Indeed and Jora.
Walk around your area with 10 printed CVs and hand them in at cafés, restaurants and shops.
Apply online to 5 listings and tailor the first sentence of each one.
Register with two temp agencies in your city.
Follow up: drop by again or write to the places where you left your CV.
Review what worked and adjust your CV, your keywords and your areas.

work.planNote: It's a pacing guide, not a rigid calendar: adjust the days to your reality.

student.text: Your student visa limits the hours you can work. Don't rely on figures people tell you: check the current conditions in VEVO and on Home Affairs, because they can change. Going over them can put your visa at risk.

whv.text: On a Working Holiday you can normally work up to 6 months with the same employer. Some work can count towards extending your visa. Confirm the exceptions before accepting a job.

work.text: Your work visa usually ties you to one employer and one occupation. Check your conditions in VEVO before accepting another job.

other.text: Check in VEVO whether your visa allows work and under what conditions before you apply.

rights: No legitimate person charges you for giving you a job or for sponsoring your visa.
Ask for a contract or offer letter and a payslip. The minimum wage applies to all workers, whatever their visa.
A trial should be short and used to assess your skills.
Be wary of offers that promise a lot of money with no experience, ask for payment upfront or run only over WhatsApp.

glossary.def: A security deposit you pay when renting. It must be lodged with your state's official body and is returned at the end of the lease if there is no damage or debt. Always ask for the receipt.
The rental contract. Read it in full before signing and keep a copy.
Housemate / shared house. It's the most common and cheapest way to rent when you arrive.
A visit to see a property before renting it. The term is also used for the landlord's periodic inspection.
Rent you pay in advance when the lease starts. The maximum allowed depends on your state.
Your tax file number. You apply for it free on the ATO website and give it to your employer.
The Australian Taxation Office.
Australian Business Number. Used by people who work for themselves (contractors), not by employees.
The retirement fund. Your employer pays money into it on top of your wages.
Your pay slip. Your employer must give you one, and it shows hours, pay, tax and super.
Gross (before tax) / net (what you receive after tax).
Work with no fixed hours, paid by the hour and normally with a loading. It's the most common arrangement in entry-level jobs.
Part-time: regular hours, fewer than full time. Full-time: full-time hours.
An agreement that sets the minimum pay and conditions for an industry (for example, hospitality). Fair Work explains it.
The Australian authority that protects workplace rights. Its phone number is 13 13 94.
A work shift / the weekly shift roster.
Walking into a business to hand in your CV in person.
A short test shift to assess your skills. If they put you to work as an employee, they must pay you.
Payment in cash. It can be legal if it's declared, but it often means no contract and no payslip: be wary.
A person who gives a reference about you (a former boss or supervisor). Employers usually ask for one or two.
The cover letter that goes with your CV.
Responsible Service of Alcohol: the certificate for serving alcohol. Each state requires it.
The safety induction certificate for working on construction sites.
A criminal record check. Some care jobs require it.
General practitioner. The first stop for almost any health issue.
Compulsory health insurance for international students (Overseas Student Health Cover).
The public health system. It doesn't cover all visitors or all visas.
When the doctor bills Medicare directly and you don't pay for the visit. It only applies if you have Medicare cover.
The government payments agency. Most temporary visas don't give access to its benefits.
An online service to check your visa and its conditions.
Confirmation of Enrolment, which international students need.
Your Home Affairs online account for visa matters.
The Office of the Migration Agents Registration Authority: the register of migration agents. Only registered agents can give immigration advice.
The arrival card you fill in before going through immigration and customs. This is where you declare food, cash and other items.
Controls to prevent pests and diseases. Declare food, plants and animal products.
Tapping your transport card when you get on and when you get off so the trip is charged correctly.
A charity second-hand shop. Cheap clothes, pots and furniture.

templates.title: Ask for advice in a Facebook group
templates.intro: For groups of migrants from your country. Post it in the group or send it as a private message.
templates.text: Hi everyone. I'm {name}, arriving in {city} on {date} on a {visa}. I'm looking for [a room / work / advice]. Could anyone already there recommend areas, transport or how to start looking for work? Thanks in advance.
templates.warn: Don't post your passport, exact address or phone number in the group. Write by private message and verify the person before sending money.

templates.title: Write to accommodation (in English)
templates.intro: For hostels, shared houses or hosts.
templates.text: Hi, my name is {name}. I'm arriving in {city} on {date} and I'm looking for a room for [number] nights. Is it still available? Could you please tell me the price, the bond (if any), what is included, and the house rules? Could I see photos or have a video call before paying? Thank you.

templates.title: Ask for work by email or message (in English)
templates.intro: To send with your CV attached to a business or a job listing.
templates.text:
Hi [name of manager],

My name is {name}. I'm looking for work as a [job title] in {city}. I have [number] years of experience in [area]. I'm available [weekdays / weekends / evenings] and can start immediately. I have the right to work in Australia (on a {visa}). I've attached my CV. Could we arrange a time to talk, or can I drop in?

Kind regards,
{name}

templates.title: Before starting a job: confirm the basics (in English)
templates.intro: Send it before your first shift so you have everything in writing.
templates.text:
Hi [name of manager],

Thanks for the opportunity. Before I start, could you please confirm my hourly rate, my days and hours, whether I will receive a payslip and super, and who my supervisor is?

Thank you,
{name}
